Actually, setting them to an empty array causes weird loading issues, so maybe that won't work, either:

```rb
> user = User.create!(checks: [])
> check = Check.create!(user: user)
> user.checks
=> []
> user.reload.checks
=> ActiveRecord::StrictLoadingViolationError:
```

@mockdeep Following are couple of ways you can bypass the strict loading mode. Maybe `strict_loading` should by default use `mode: n_plus_one_only` instead of `:all` in order to make it easier but I do not have the depth in this matter and would leave to the Rails core team to decide. Happy to debug more if that makes sense  to the Rails team 😊. 

1. Disable `strict_loading` on user object
```
user = User.create!
user.strict_loading!(false)

user.checks # => should work.
```

2. Enable `strict_loading` in `n_plus_one_only` mode only(**I would recommend this**)
```
user = User.create!
user.strict_loading!(mode: :n_plus_one_only)

user.checks # => should work.
user.checks.first.some_assocation_name # => should raise exception
```

3. Disable `strict_loading` on `checks` association(model level)
```
class User < ApplicationRecord
  self.strict_loading_by_default = true

  has_many :checks, strict_loading: false
end
```

issue.title: ActiveRecord#strict_loading! should return boolean instead of current mode set.
issue.body:
The return type was changed in the PR #41704 after addition of mode
option. The current documentation is misleading since
documentation propose strict_loading! would return boolean whereas
it returns the current mode set.

I came across this issue while debugging: #41827 and thought
this should be brought to the attention.

PR fixes the issue and would always return boolean based on
strict_loading is enabled or disabled.

```
user.strict_loading! # => true
user.strict_loading!(false) # => false
user.strict_loading!(mode: :n_plus_one_only) # => true
```

